editorial.headline: Beyond the Build: Finishing Work That Makes a Building Complete
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans the fitted, decorative and practical finishing work that turns a construction project into a usable, recognisable space.
editorial.body:
This activity covers the building-finishing work that sits beyond the main structure: installing and dismantling exhibition stands; fitting built-in kitchens, stairs, shop fittings and furniture; installing garden equipment; and placing exterior decorative mouldings, cornices and façades. It also reaches interior decoration and ornamental or artistic installation work. The common thread is completion: the specialist work that gives a building its functional fittings, its visual character and its final public face.

Registration is open across the full business-scale range—micro, small, medium and large. That matters because the activity is not confined to a single type of commercial operation or project size. A business working within this scope can be registered at the scale appropriate to its enterprise, while the scope itself remains focused on these specified finishing and installation activities. The boundary is practical as much as aesthetic: it concerns the elements installed, fitted, assembled or removed as part of completing a building environment.

At the national level, foreign investment is open for this activity and foreign ownership is permitted up to 100%. That is a clear position, not a partial opening: the national foreign-ownership ceiling does not impose a lower cap. For a foreign-owned business, the relevant question is therefore not whether foreign participation is allowed in principle, but whether the planned work genuinely falls within the stated finishing scope—from exhibition installations and fitted interiors to exterior ornamental treatment and façades.

Bali’s position is also open in the record, rather than blocked. The province-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for low- and medium-low-risk activities, but this activity is not blocked by that rule. At the large-business scale, its OSS risk assessment is medium-high or high, which places it outside the moratorium’s blocked category. In plain terms, a foreign investor can register this activity in Bali today, subject to the scope and scale reflected in the record; Bali does not add a separate foreign-ownership cap or partnership condition here.
editorial.pullQuote: In Bali, this activity is not caught by the PMA moratorium because its large-scale OSS risk is medium-high or high.
